facts.fact_text: The applicants wished to hold an assembly (a march) in Warsaw within the framework of Equality Days organised by the Foundation for Equality, planned for 10-12 June 2005.
On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.
The march on 11 June 2005 was attended by approximately 3,000 people.
The march on 11 June 2005 was protected by the police.
In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants argued that the assemblies were to be entirely peaceful and that banning them breached their freedom of assembly guaranteed by the Constitution.
In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants submitted that the assemblies did not pose any threat to either public order or morals.
On 3 June 2005 the Traffic Officer, acting on behalf of the Mayor of Warsaw, refused permission for the march.

The Traffic Officer's refusal of permission for the march on 3 June 2005 was based on the organisers' failure to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') within the meaning of Article 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act.
The Traffic Officer alleged that the organisers had been ordered to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') prior to the refusal of 3 June 2005.

In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the requirement to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' lacked any legal basis.
In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the applicants had never been requested to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' prior to the refusal of 3 June 2005.

The Local Government Appeals Board found that the first-instance authority's decision of 3 June 2005 referred to the absence of a traffic organisation plan in the case file, but that the case file contained no mention that the organisers had been obliged to submit such a plan.

The Local Government Appeals Board found that the document on the procedure for obtaining permission to organise an event which was served on the organisers contained no information on the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the requirement to submit a permit to occupy a part of the road, based on the provisions of the Road Traffic Act, lacked any legal basis in the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act.

Under section 65 of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, the organisers of sporting events, contests, assemblies and other events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to obtain permission for the organisation of such assemblies.

Under section 65 read together with section 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, organisers of events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to comply with various administrative obligations specified in a list contained in section 65(a), numbering nineteen items, including the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan to the authorities.

In his decision of 9 June 2005 banning the stationary assemblies, the Mayor of Warsaw relied on the argument that assemblies held under the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act (Ustawa o zgromadzeniach) had to be organised away from roads used for road traffic.
In his decision of 9 June 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that if assemblies were to use roads, more stringent requirements applied.

The Mazowsze Governor observed that a decision banning an assembly had to be regarded as a method of last resort because it radically restricted freedom of expression.

The Mazowsze Governor observed that the principle of proportionality required that any restriction of constitutionally protected freedoms be permitted only in so far as it was dictated by the concrete circumstances of a particular case.
